title: Repeating patterns: how to find the minimum period

sources.name: NCETM — Pattern: identifying the unit of repeat

practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.html:
The minimum period is the length of the smallest block that repeats to make a repeating pattern. In ABABAB, that block is AB, so the minimum period is 2.

Ready for a puzzle? Try the Reasoning Challenge, with patterns, numbers, shapes and logic.

The block is also called the unit of repeat. Think of a striped scarf: you want the little sequence the knitter keeps using, not a description of the whole scarf.
sections.title: What is the minimum period of a pattern?

sections.html:
1. Choose a short block from the start of the pattern.
  2. Repeat it and compare every item with the row you were given.
  3. If anything differs, try a longer block. The first length that works is the minimum period.

For AABAABAAB, A alone fails when you reach B. AA fails there too. But AAB | AAB | AAB matches all nine letters, giving a minimum period of 3.

NCETM’s pattern guide explains why identifying the smallest unit is the useful step.
sections.title: Try the shortest block first

sections.html:
Repeat circle–square–circle and you get circle–square–circle | circle–square–circle. Two circles meet at the join. That pair is part of the rule, not an error.

Likewise, ABAB is a block you could repeat to make ABABABAB, but it is not the smallest: AB already works.
sections.title: The join can fool you

sections.html:
B, if the rule is to repeat ABB. Group it as ABB | ABB | AB. The last group is missing its final B; the displayed row can stop partway through a repeat.

A short row can fit several rules, so check the puzzle’s instructions. A growing pattern such as 2, 4, 6, 8 needs a different explanation. Next, try checking every step in a number pattern or the Reasoning Challenge.
